endorsements.quote: Psychological safety should be added to this list as a first-class release criterion: models should be benchmarked for sycophancy, excessive anthropomorphisation, and delusion reinforcement prior to release, with results published in model cards so that claims of safety are auditable rather than taken on trust.
Developers should additionally provide accessible mechanisms for users and families to report harmful model behaviour, feeding the same surveillance loop.

Existing post-market surveillance infrastructure, such as the MHRA Yellow Card scheme, could be adapted to capture AI-related mental health harms, creating a formal reporting channel equivalent to that for adverse drug reactions [30].

unlisted_practices: Ask clinicians assessing new-onset psychosis, mania, or marked behavioural change to routinely ask about AI chatbot use and document positive findings in a structured way.
Incorporate a structured technological history into psychiatric assessment covering AI systems used, duration and timing of use, anthropomorphisation, and functional impact.

Develop a standardised working definition of AI-associated psychosis through formal consensus methodology such as a Delphi process involving psychiatrists, AI researchers, and people with lived experience.
Establish case registries and longitudinal cohorts to study AI-associated psychosis and derive a consensus case definition.
Develop systems to detect sycophantic and delusion-reinforcing model behaviour and refine benchmarks measuring propensity to co-construct delusional content.
Have frontier technology companies collaborate with clinicians and researchers on post-release surveillance to detect high-risk conversational trajectories and steer users away from them.
Expand reporting guidelines such as CONSORT-AI to cover sycophancy and psychological safety outcomes in trials of AI-based interventions.
Establish regulatory frameworks specifying disclosure requirements, third-party audit rights, and incident notification duties for sycophantic and delusional AI outputs.
Empirically study trade-offs between safety, utility, and privacy of technical interventions such as system prompt changes, guardrails, session length limits, and fine-tuning changes.
Include diverse cultural and non-English-speaking populations in case data on AI-associated psychosis.

screen.reason: Perspective/commentary examining whether AI psychosis should be a clinical entity and providing recommendations for clinicians, developers, and regulators on safeguards and surveillance.
